summary: The admin side is the real product; the student app is the shop window. Three hard constraints dominate. (1) Immutability: every serious item bank (Moodle, Canvas, QTI-conformant systems) versions items rather than mutating them — a quiz/attempt must pin a specific item version, because psychometric statistics and score defensibility are only valid against the exact rendered version. (2) Ingestion economics: math OCR is the bottleneck, and the 2026 price/accuracy frontier is Mathpix Convert API at $0.002/image and $0.005/PDF-page (verified vendor pricing) versus open-source Surya 2 (650M params, olmOCR-bench 83.3, 5.35 pages/s on an RTX 5090) whose *weights* are Rail-M-licensed and free only for startups under $5M funding/revenue — a commercial licence is required past that, which most teams miss. Generic Document AI (Google Read $0.65/1k pages, Azure Read $1.50/1k pages) is the wrong tool: neither emits LaTeX. The realistic 2026 pipeline is a two-stage hybrid: Mathpix or Surya for layout+LaTeX, then a vision LLM pass to segment the page into structured question JSON (options, answer key, diagram crops). (3) Psychometrics as a first-class schema, not a report: QTI 3.0's Usage Data spec already gives a ready-made vocabulary (P-value, PTbis, A/B/C/D-Param, AIS, plus per-distractor NumberChoosingResponse/PercentChoosingResponse/AISResponse/PTbis-Response) that maps almost 1:1 onto Postgres tables. Empirical thresholds are well established (discrimination ≤0.20 poor, ≥0.35 excellent; non-functioning distractor <5% selection), but a 2025 study of 14,238 items found static thresholds caught only 85.7% of genuinely flawed items — so auto-flagging must route to a human reviewer queue, never auto-retire. The two-role RBAC model (ADMIN/STUDENT) is the single biggest architectural mistake in the brief: an item bank at 10k-student scale needs at minimum AUTHOR, REVIEWER, SUBJECT_LEAD (approver), OPS/SUPPORT and ANALYST, because "who approved this item" is the audit trail you need when a student disputes a mock-test key. Copyright is more favourable than expected for exam use specifically — Section 52(1)(i) of the Indian Copyright Act 1957 exempts reproduction "as part of the questions to be answered in an examination" — but that exemption does not cleanly extend to a commercial app republishing whole PYQ papers with solutions, and coaching-institute material is straightforwardly infringing. Bilingual is a hard NTA requirement (13 NEET languages; bilingual booklet with English authoritative on translation ambiguity), which means language must be a column on the item, not a separate item.

findings.title: Mathpix Convert API: exact 2026 pricing and hard limits
findings.detail: Verified from vendor pricing page. Image service (v3/text, v3/latex, v3/batch): $0.002/image for 0–1M images, $0.0015/image beyond 1M. PDF service (v3/pdf): $0.005/page for 0–1M pages, $0.0035/page beyond. One-time $19.99 setup fee; $29 free testing credit on account creation; billed 1st of month. Strokes: free to 1K sessions, then $0.01/session. Limits: 5 MB JSON body for image endpoints, 512 KB for v3/strokes, 1 GB PDF upload, 10 MB image download from URL with 15s timeout; Files API allows 15 GB/file and 200,000 files/job. Quota exceeded returns HTTP 429 with error ID `http_max_requests`. Monthly quotas are configurable via `image_monthly_limit` and `page_monthly_limit`; the page quota is SHARED between v3/pdf and the Files API. Per-minute per-app and per-IP rate limits exist but vary by plan and are not published. Snip (end-user app) Pro from $4.99/mo; Files API from $1.00/1k pages. Mathpix states it processes >10M images/day at 99.9%+ uptime but publishes NO accuracy percentage.
findings.implication: Budget: ingesting 50,000 scanned coaching pages costs ~$250 via v3/pdf — trivially affordable, so build-vs-buy should not be decided on API cost. The real cost is human verification. The shared page quota between v3/pdf and Files API is a trap for a bulk-ingest admin tool that uses both. Because Mathpix publishes no accuracy figure, do not promise admins an accuracy SLA; instead instrument your own per-batch correction rate.

findings.title: Open-source math OCR: real benchmark numbers, throughput, and a licence trap
findings.detail: olmOCR-Bench = 1,403 PDFs / 7,010 unit tests with strict visual-equivalence checks on LaTeX via KaTeX DOM bounding boxes. Current leaderboard (late 2025 / 2026): Infinity-Parser2-Pro 87.6, chandra-ocr-2 85.8, dots.mocr 83.9, surya-ocr-2 83.3, LightOnOCR-2-1B 83.2. Surya 2: 650M params, 90+ languages, returns equations wrapped in <math>...</math>, 5.35 pages/s on RTX 5090 (vllm, concurrency 128, 32 GB VRAM) vs 0.108 pages/s on Apple Silicon via llama.cpp. Marker (built on Surya): balanced mode 76.0 overall on olmOCR-bench and 83.5 on born-digital PDFs, fast mode 66.6; throughput on a single B200: 2.9 pages/s balanced, 7.4 fast, 23.7 fast-no-OCR; outputs Markdown/JSON/HTML/chunks with LaTeX equations; `--use_llm` and `--redo_inline_math` hybrid mode delegates inline math to Gemini/Claude/OpenAI/Ollama for highest quality. LICENCE TRAP: for both Surya and Marker the CODE is Apache 2.0 but the WEIGHTS are a modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M licence, free only for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue — a paid commercial licence is required above that. pix2tex/LaTeX-OCR is MIT and unencumbered but reports only BLEU 0.88, normalised edit distance 0.10, token accuracy 0.60, and handles single formulas, not full pages.
findings.implication: A self-hosted Marker/Surya ingest worker on one GPU processes ~10k pages/hour — enough to digitise an entire coaching institute's archive in days. But the Rail-M weight licence means a funded ed-tech company must either buy a commercial licence or fall back to MIT-licensed pix2tex (formula-only, materially worse) or a paid API. Token accuracy of 0.60 for pix2tex means ~40% of formulas need an edit — unusable without a review UI. Budget for a GPU worker on GCP (the brief already includes GCP) rather than trying to OCR on Supabase Edge Functions, which have no GPU.

findings.title: Vision-LLM ingestion is now cost-competitive and is the only approach that produces structured question JSON in one pass
findings.detail: 2026 aggregator benchmarks: Gemini 3 Flash ~$0.50/M input + $3.00/M output tokens, working out to roughly $2.25 per 1,000 pages for OCR/extraction; a 200-page document costs ~$0.73 on Gemini vs ~$0.98 on Claude. At 1,000 × 50-page documents: Gemini ~$24, Claude ~$270, GPT ~$218; Batch APIs cut all of these ~50%. Claude Sonnet 4.6 reported at 97.6% field-extraction accuracy, ~3.8 points above Gemini on complex documents. These figures come from third-party comparison blogs, not vendor benchmark pages — treat the accuracy numbers as indicative, not audited. Crucially, dedicated OCR (Mathpix, Surya) returns a page of markup; a vision LLM can return {stem_latex, options[4], correct_index, chapter_guess, difficulty_guess, has_diagram, diagram_bbox, pyq_year} in one call.
findings.implication: The right architecture is two-stage, not either/or: (1) Mathpix or Surya for high-fidelity LaTeX and layout, (2) a vision-LLM pass over the page image PLUS the OCR text to segment into individual items and populate metadata. Feeding the LLM both the image and the OCR text materially reduces LaTeX hallucination versus image-only. At ~$2/1k pages the LLM stage is not the cost driver; it is a rounding error against editor salaries. Use Batch API for archival back-catalogue ingestion (50% saving, latency irrelevant) and sync calls only for the admin's interactive 'paste a page, get questions' flow.

findings.title: Generic Document AI (Google/Azure) is the wrong tool for STEM items — pricing confirms it is priced for forms, not formulas
findings.detail: Google Document AI 2026: Read API (OCR only) $0.65/1,000 pages; Layout and prebuilt models $10/1,000 pages; Custom Extraction $30/1,000 pages; neural model training $3/hour after 10 free hours/month. Azure Document Intelligence 2026: Read $1.50/1,000 pages; Layout $10/1,000; Prebuilt $10/1,000; Custom Extraction $30/1,000; same $3/hour training. Reported hidden overhead of 25–40% (GCP) and 25–35% (Azure) once storage, orchestration and 40–80 hours of integration engineering are counted. Neither service emits LaTeX or MathML for inline mathematics — they are optimised for invoices, receipts, W-2s and forms.
findings.implication: Do not use Document AI for question ingestion. It would be defensible only for a non-question admin flow — e.g. bulk-parsing student ID documents or institutional enrolment forms. The $30/1k Custom Extraction tier is 15× Mathpix's PDF rate for a worse result on mathematics. Since the stack already includes GCP, the sensible GCP role is GPU compute for a self-hosted Marker/Surya worker plus Cloud Storage, not Document AI.

findings.title: QTI 3.0 Usage Data spec is a ready-made psychometrics schema — copy it verbatim into Postgres
findings.detail: The 1EdTech QTI 3.0 Usage Data & Item Statistics binding defines exactly the vocabulary an admin analytics layer needs. Ordinary (item-level) statistics: A-Param (IRT discrimination), B-Param (IRT difficulty), C-Param (guessing/lower asymptote), D-Param (dispersion), P-value (percent answering correctly — explicitly noted as group-dependent), AIS (average item score), PTbis (point-biserial), PHI, rbis (biserial), Polyserial, Score_Conversion, and Fifths_Table variants (Highest, Second_Highest, Middle, Second_Lowest, Lowest). Categorized (per-distractor) statistics: NumberChoosingResponse, PercentChoosingResponse, AISResponse, PTbis-Response. XML root element is `usageData` with `ordinaryStatistic` and `categorizedStatistic` children; attributes are name (required), context (URI identifying the population/administration the statistic was computed over), glossary, caseCount, stdError, stdDeviation, lastUpdated. Statistics attach via `targetObject` with identifier, optional partIdentifier, and objectType ∈ {test, testpart, section, item, outcome, interaction, choice}.
findings.implication: Model item statistics as (item_version_id, context_id, statistic_name, value, case_count, std_error, computed_at) rather than as columns on the questions table. The `context` attribute is the critical design lesson: the same item has different P-values for JEE Main vs NEET cohorts and for 2025 vs 2026 batches, so statistics must be scoped to a cohort/administration, never global. objectType also legitimises attaching statistics to a whole test, a section, or a single choice — which is exactly what distractor analysis needs. Adopting these names verbatim gives free QTI export later and stops the team inventing a private vocabulary.

findings.title: QTI 3.0 deliberately EXCLUDES authored 'difficulty' from its metadata profile — authored difficulty and empirical difficulty must be separate fields
findings.detail: The QTI 3.0 Metadata binding profiles IEEE LOM but explicitly excludes the LOM fields 'Interactivity Type', 'Difficulty' and 'Typical Age Range' as unsuitable for assessment resources. QTI-specific metadata elements that ARE defined: itemTemplate (boolean — item varies by random/external factors), timeDependent (boolean — scoring considers attempt duration), composite (boolean — multiple interactions in one item), interactionType (unbounded enumeration of 22 types including choiceInteraction, textEntryInteraction, extendedTextInteraction), portableCustomInteractionContext, feedbackType (adaptive|nonadaptive|none), solutionAvailable (boolean), scoringMode (human|externalmachine|responseprocessing), and toolName/toolVersion/toolVendor (String256). LOM sections retained: General (Identifier, Title, Language, Description, Keyword), Lifecycle (Version, Status, Contribute), Technical, Educational (Learning Resource Type restricted to exercise/questionnaire, Context, Typical Learning Time), Rights (Cost, Copyright, Description), Classification.
findings.implication: The brief's content model tags questions by 'difficulty'. Split this into two columns: `authored_difficulty` (EASY/MEDIUM/HARD, set by the author, used for blueprint assembly before any attempt data exists) and `empirical_difficulty_p` (computed, per-cohort, authoritative once caseCount ≥ threshold). Admin UI should show both side by side — the delta is itself a quality signal, and a systematic gap tells you an author mis-calibrates. Also adopt Lifecycle.Status for the editorial workflow state and Rights.Copyright for provenance (see the copyright finding) — both are standard fields you would otherwise invent. `timeDependent` and `Typical Learning Time` map directly onto the per-question expected-time field you need for the student-facing time analytics.

findings.title: Concrete item-flagging thresholds, and hard evidence that static thresholds alone are insufficient
findings.detail: Rezigalla et al. 2024 bands: difficulty index — easy ≥78%, acceptable 26–75%, difficult <25%. Discrimination index — poor ≤0.20, acceptable 0.21–0.24, good 0.25–0.34, excellent ≥0.35. Non-functioning distractor (NFD) defined as any distractor selected by <5% of examinees; distractor efficiency graded excellent (0 NFDs), good (1), acceptable (2), poor (3). Distractor efficiency correlates negatively with difficulty (r = −0.548, p = 0.000) and with discrimination (r = −0.259, p = 0.0476). A 2025 six-year study (Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University) analysed 14,238 items across 236 exams (2017–2022) using p-value < 0.25 OR point-biserial < 0 as auto-flag rules: 0.6% of all items ultimately required correction, but 25% of exams contained at least one flawed item. Detection performance: the combined thresholds caught ~85.7% of genuinely flawed items and MISSED 14.3% (which had p ≥ 0.25 and r_pb ≥ 0); p-value alone caught ~80%, point-biserial alone only ~50%. Authors conclude static thresholds are insufficient and must be paired with expert review. Separately, in CTT practice distractors are flagged when chosen by <5% (non-functioning) or >30% (over-attractive), and the correct option should have positive point-biserial while every distractor should have negative point-biserial — a distractor with positive point-biserial is the classic signature of a miskeyed item.
findings.implication: Ship an auto-flag rule engine with these exact defaults, but wire it to a REVIEW QUEUE, not to auto-retirement. Concretely: flag if (p < 0.25) OR (r_pb < 0) OR (any distractor r_pb > correct-option r_pb → suspected miskey) OR (any distractor selected <5% → dead distractor) OR (any distractor selected >30% AND is not the key → ambiguity). Gate all of it behind caseCount ≥ 100 for stable classical statistics. Set expectations with stakeholders using the 0.6%/25% figures: a mature bank yields very few broken items, but almost every full-length mock will contain one — so the SLA is 'flagged within 24h of the test closing', not 'zero flawed items'.

findings.title: Test-level reliability: alpha ≥0.80 is the high-stakes bar, and SEM is arguably the better metric to surface to admins
findings.detail: Nunnally (1978) established 0.70 as the lowest acceptable reliability for basic research and 0.80 as adequate; >0.80 good, >0.90 excellent. For examinations the traditionally accepted minimum is 0.80, described as the benchmark below which an exam or elements within it should not fall. SEM (standard error of measurement) is a direct function of alpha: SEM = SD × sqrt(1 − alpha). Analysis of MRCP(UK) examinations argues SEM is a more appropriate quality measure than reliability for postgraduate assessment, because alpha is inflated by test length and by the spread of the candidate population. Note the 0.70 convention has been criticised as a flawed metric for diagnostic assessments.
findings.implication: Compute Cronbach's alpha (or KR-20 for dichotomous items) per test AND per section, and display SEM in raw-mark units next to it — SEM is what actually answers an admin's question 'is this student's rank trustworthy?'. Critical caveat for this product: alpha rises with item count, so a 25-question chapter practice set will show a much lower alpha than a 180-question full NEET mock, and admins WILL misread that as a quality regression. Either normalise via Spearman-Brown or refuse to display alpha below a minimum item count (~20). Also compute alpha on a per-cohort basis — a homogeneous top-rankers-only batch will show depressed alpha through range restriction, not through bad items.

findings.title: Item versioning: Moodle's model is the reference implementation to copy
findings.detail: In Moodle 4.5 every edit or update to a question creates a new version; the version number is visible in the question bank, and 'History' in the Actions dropdown lists all versions, each of which can be previewed, edited and deleted independently. In Moodle 4.5 and earlier, questions live in one question bank per course organised into categories/subcategories at course, course-category or system context, and changes to a question are reflected everywhere it is used. Moodle 5.0 (2025) changed this substantially: a course can now hold multiple named question banks under Course navigation > More > Question banks, and questions previously held in course context are migrated into an auto-created '[Course name] shared question bank' on upgrade — an upgrade that has caused visible user reports of banks appearing empty or relocating. QTI 3.0 best practice reinforces the identity discipline: the identifier attribute must be a non-null unique string, and organisations should add organisational prefixes to identifiers to guarantee uniqueness across vendors.
findings.implication: Copy Moodle's version-history model, but make one improvement Moodle only partially enforces: a delivered test must reference a specific `question_version_id`, never a mutable `question_id`. Schema: `questions` (stable identity, slug with org prefix) → `question_versions` (immutable content, version_no, status, created_by, approved_by, published_at) → `test_questions` (pins question_version_id) → `attempts.responses` (pins question_version_id). This makes 'never mutate a question that has been attempted' a foreign-key invariant rather than a policy. Practical rule to encode: an edit that changes the stem, any option, or the key MUST fork a new version and reset all statistics; a metadata-only edit (chapter re-tag, PYQ year correction, typo in the solution text) may update in place. Also learn from Moodle 5.0's painful migration: get the bank-scoping model right before you have 50,000 items, because rehoming a question bank later is a support nightmare.

findings.title: Section 52(1)(i) of the Indian Copyright Act 1957 — exact statutory wording for the exam exemption
findings.detail: Verbatim: "the reproduction of any work—(i) by a teacher or a pupil in the course of instruction; or (ii) as part of the questions to be answered in an examination; or (iii) in answers to such questions" is not an infringement of copyright. This is the education/examination carve-out in Section 52(1)(i). Section 52 as a whole is a purpose-specific limitation covering private/personal use including research, criticism, review, reporting of current events, judicial proceedings and education — India follows enumerated 'fair dealing', not open-ended US-style 'fair use', so a purpose not listed is not exempt regardless of how transformative or non-commercial it is.
findings.implication: Three distinct legal postures, which the product must model as a `source_provenance` field on every item: (a) ORIGINAL — authored in-house, fully owned, no risk; (b) PYQ — a genuine previous-year JEE/NEET question. These are published by NTA at nta.ac.in/Downloads for free public download, and reproducing an exam question 'as part of the questions to be answered in an examination' sits closest to the statutory exemption. However, a commercial subscription app is NOT a teacher, and reproducing an entire past paper wholesale with commentary is publishing, not instruction — so treat PYQs as low-but-nonzero risk and never as certainly clear. (c) THIRD-PARTY COACHING MATERIAL (Allen, Aakash, FIITJEE, Resonance, PW question banks, and their solution PDFs) — original literary works owned by those institutes; copying is straightforward infringement with no plausible Section 52 defence for a competing commercial product. Enforce this in the admin UI: ingestion from a scanned coaching PDF must force the uploader to declare provenance, and items marked as third-party-sourced must be blocked from publish until rewritten and re-approved.

findings.title: Bilingual/multilingual is a hard NTA requirement with specific semantics, not a nice-to-have
findings.detail: NEET UG is offered in 13 media: English, Hindi, Urdu, plus Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu. Candidates choosing English receive an English-only booklet; candidates choosing any other medium receive a BILINGUAL test booklet containing every question in both the chosen language and English. Official rule: "In case of any ambiguity in translation, the English version is considered final." Language availability is geographically restricted by centre state — Assamese only in Assam; Bengali in West Bengal, Tripura and Andaman & Nicobar; Gujarati in Gujarat, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli; Kannada in Karnataka; Malayalam in Kerala and Lakshadweep; Marathi in Maharashtra; Odia in Odisha; Punjabi in Punjab, Chandigarh and Delhi; Tamil in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry; Telugu in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; English/Hindi/Urdu nationwide. Medium is fixed at registration and cannot be changed. QTI 3.0 best practice for multilingual items is the xml:lang attribute plus bidirectional text (bdo) support, and shared passages are referenced via qti-assessment-stimulus-ref rather than duplicated per item.
findings.implication: Data model consequence: translations are versioned children of a question_version, NOT sibling questions — schema `question_version_translations (question_version_id, lang_code, stem, options[], solution, translated_by, reviewed_by, status)`, with a DB constraint that a translation cannot be published unless its parent English version is published, and that editing the English version invalidates (does not silently keep) all translations. Encode 'English is authoritative' literally: the answer key, marks and correct_index live ONLY on the English row; translations carry presentation text only. Render bilingually in the same screen (English block above regional block) to mirror the real booklet rather than as a language toggle — students sit the real exam in that format. JEE Main is bilingual English/Hindi plus regional options; NEET's 13 languages make full coverage a 13× editorial cost, so scope Hindi+English at launch and treat regional languages as a per-state expansion decision driven by the geographic restriction table above.

findings.title: Blueprint-driven automated test assembly is a solved optimisation problem — use MILP, not ad-hoc SQL
findings.detail: Automated Test Assembly (ATA) is standard practice in large-scale standardised assessment. It formulates test construction as an optimisation problem with binary item-selection variables, solved by mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) or greedy heuristics. Constraints routinely encoded: content balancing (N items per chapter/topic), test length, target difficulty/information curve, item-type quotas, inter-form overlap, item exposure control, answer-key balancing (so the key is not disproportionately option C), and word count. The Big Shadow Test (BST) method with MIP is described as the most representative approach because it accommodates complex practical constraints. There is an active literature debate (van der Linden & Li 2016 and rejoinders) on whether heuristics remain necessary now that MIP solvers are fast.
findings.implication: For 10k concurrent students, the constraint set is: exactly N per chapter per the JEE/NEET blueprint, difficulty distribution (e.g. 30/50/20 easy/medium/hard by empirical p, falling back to authored_difficulty for uncalibrated items), zero items used in the student's last 3 tests, PYQ-year spread, and key balancing. This is a small MILP — a few thousand binary variables — solvable in well under a second with OR-Tools CP-SAT or HiGHS in a Python/Node worker; do NOT attempt it in Postgres. CRITICAL interaction with the brief's 'randomised question order per student': randomising ORDER is safe and preserves rank comparability. Randomising CONTENT (giving different students different items) breaks fair comparison and ranking unless you either (a) assemble parallel forms with matched statistical targets and then equate scores, or (b) keep the item set identical and shuffle only presentation order and option order. For a leaderboard product, the correct default is: identical item set for a given mock, shuffled item order and shuffled options per student, seeded deterministically by (test_id, user_id) so it is reproducible for dispute resolution. Store the seed, not the permutation.

findings.title: Two roles is insufficient — the argument for AUTHOR / REVIEWER / SUBJECT_LEAD / OPS / ANALYST
findings.detail: Serious assessment platforms separate authoring from approval as a matter of course. Item banking vendors emphasise that as items are revised and versioned it is imperative that changes in content AND the users who made them are tracked, because if a test is challenged as unfair it can be critical to maintain question versions and the construction history of each question. TAO ships Authoring, Reporting, Rostering & Delivery and Grader as distinct modules with distinct access. QTI 3.0 carries LOM Lifecycle.Status and Lifecycle.Contribute (contributor role + entity + date) as first-class item metadata. Moodle exposes item status (draft/ready) alongside version history. Note: I could not retrieve a vendor page enumerating a canonical role list — the specific five-role decomposition below is my synthesis, not a cited standard.
findings.implication: Argue FOR a richer role set, but implement it as capabilities, not as a role enum. Minimum viable decomposition: AUTHOR (create/edit DRAFT versions in own subject, cannot publish), REVIEWER (peer review, can request changes, cannot approve own authored items), SUBJECT_LEAD/SME (approve → PUBLISHED, retire items, sole holder of the publish capability for a subject), OPS/SUPPORT (triage student 'report this question' flags, cannot edit content, can escalate), ANALYST (read-only across all analytics, no content mutation), plus SUPER_ADMIN. The single non-negotiable rule is separation of duties: the author of a version cannot be its approver — enforce with a CHECK constraint (approved_by <> created_by), not UI logic. In Supabase this is roles in raw_app_meta_data (admin-controlled) feeding RLS policies; do NOT use raw_user_meta_data, which is user-modifiable. Item lifecycle states: DRAFT → IN_REVIEW → CHANGES_REQUESTED → APPROVED → PUBLISHED → FLAGGED → RETIRED, with RETIRED items remaining permanently readable because past attempts reference them.

findings.title: Supabase RLS performance rules that determine whether the admin console survives a 50k-item bank
findings.detail: Documented Supabase benchmarks: wrapping auth functions in a subselect — `using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id)` instead of `using (auth.uid() = user_id)` — yields 94–99% improvement by enabling Postgres initPlan caching (evaluated once per statement, not once per row). Adding a btree index on any column referenced in a policy: 99.94% improvement. Always specifying `TO authenticated` on policies: 99.78% improvement by skipping policy evaluation for anon. Duplicating the policy's filter in the client query (`.eq('user_id', userId)` rather than a bare `.select()`): 94.74% improvement. Rewriting policies to avoid joins back to the source table — `WHERE team_id IN (SELECT team_id FROM team_user WHERE user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()))` instead of joining — 99.78% improvement. SECURITY DEFINER functions bypass RLS on their contents for privileged joins but must never be exposed in a public schema. Roles belong in raw_app_meta_data (admin-controlled), never raw_user_meta_data (user-modifiable). JWT claims are cached until token refresh, so role/permission changes do not take effect until the token is renewed. Supabase advises against policy lists exceeding ~1,000 items without redesign. auth.uid() returns null when unauthenticated, so `USING (auth.uid() IS NOT NULL AND ...)` avoids silent failures.
findings.implication: Two direct consequences. (1) The JWT caching behaviour means revoking an author's publish capability does not take effect until their token refreshes — for a destructive capability like PUBLISH or RETIRE, check the role against the database inside a SECURITY DEFINER RPC rather than trusting the JWT claim. (2) An admin browsing a 50k-item bank with per-subject RLS will hit the join-in-policy antipattern immediately; precompute a `user_subject_access(user_id, subject_id)` table and write the policy as `subject_id IN (SELECT subject_id FROM user_subject_access WHERE user_id = (select auth.uid()))`. Index question_versions on (subject_id, status, updated_at) — the admin list view's natural sort.

findings.title: Duplicate detection: three complementary layers, none sufficient alone
findings.detail: For text/LaTeX near-duplicates: MinHash + LSH estimates Jaccard similarity from compact signatures rather than O(n²) pairwise comparison; 2025 work reports SIMD vectorisation giving 7× speedup on the intersection step and end-to-end dedup latency dropping from hours to seconds. Industry practice combines approximate matching (MinHash LSH / Jaccard) for lexical near-duplicates with semantic matching via vector embeddings for meaning-level duplicates. For images (diagrams, scanned question crops): the imagehash library provides aHash (luminance), pHash (FFT/DCT structural), dHash (pixel gradient), wHash (wavelet), colorhash (HSV distribution, position-independent) and a crop-resistant variant; default hashsize=8 gives a 64-bit hash compared by Hamming distance with a tunable threshold; the defining property is that similar inputs produce similar hashes, unlike cryptographic hashing. No quantified accuracy figures are published for imagehash — thresholds must be tuned empirically on your own corpus.
findings.implication: Implement three layers at ingest time, all surfaced as a 'possible duplicate' warning in the authoring UI rather than a hard block. Layer 1 — exact: SHA-256 of a normalised stem (LaTeX canonicalised, whitespace/case stripped, numbers preserved) catches straight re-uploads instantly. Layer 2 — lexical near-duplicate: MinHash-LSH over character 5-grams of the normalised stem, Jaccard ≥ ~0.8, which catches the classic 'same PYQ, different coaching institute's transcription'. Layer 3 — semantic: pgvector embedding of stem+options with cosine ≥ ~0.92, which catches numerically-varied clones of the same physics problem (same setup, different values) — a very common pattern in Indian coaching material and arguably a feature (variant families) rather than a defect. For scanned/image questions, dHash or pHash at hashsize=16 with a Hamming threshold you calibrate on ~500 known pairs. Model the outcome as a `question_relations` table with kind ∈ {EXACT_DUPLICATE, NEAR_DUPLICATE, VARIANT_OF, SUPERSEDES} so 'variant family' becomes exploitable in test assembly (never put two variants of the same problem in one paper).

findings.title: TAO and the open-source item-banking landscape as a build reference
findings.detail: TAO (taotesting.com) splits into Authoring ('build feature-rich online assessments based on open education standards'), Reporting, Rostering & Delivery, and Cloud Services on GCP/AWS, plus TAO Advance (delivery engine), TAO Grader (manual scoring) and TAO Insights (API data access). Licensing is a Community Edition (free, open source) plus three commercial tiers — Accelerate, Ignite, Enterprise — priced by user volume. Marketing explicitly names 'easy tools, 21st-century item banking, and smart workflows', custom interactions, multimedia, accommodations and WCAG compliance. The site does not publish which QTI version is supported nor an explicit author/reviewer/approver role breakdown.
findings.implication: TAO Community Edition is the closest open-source analogue to what the admin side must become, and is worth installing purely to steal its authoring IA (item form layout, bank navigation, test-part/section builder) rather than to adopt as a dependency — it is PHP/Java and cannot be embedded in a Supabase + React Native stack. The four-module split (Authoring / Reporting / Rostering & Delivery / Grading) is a good top-level navigation model for the admin console. Note the separate 'Grader' module: even in a pure-MCQ product you will eventually need manual review of numeric-answer (JEE Main NAT-type) responses where tolerance and significant-figure rules are contested.

findings.title: QTI 3.0 structural concepts worth adopting even without full QTI compliance
findings.detail: QTI 3.0 requires a test to contain at least one testPart and every part to contain at least one section, with nested sections supported — this maps directly onto sectioned JEE/NEET papers. Choice-order randomisation is a native `shuffle` attribute on choiceInteraction. Non-linear/adaptive progression uses branch rules and preconditions. Shared reading passages or shared diagrams are referenced via `qti-assessment-stimulus-ref` and packaged once, shared across many items, rather than duplicated. The spec notes that the time a candidate is given to respond 'is important for the psychometric properties' of an item, and delivery systems enforce attempt duration limits. QTI 3.0's headline changes over 2.2 are transform-free authoring-to-delivery, HTML5-native markup, integrated APIP accessibility, and native Computer Adaptive Testing support; Portable Custom Interactions (PCI) cover technology-enhanced item types.
findings.implication: Adopt the testPart → section → item hierarchy verbatim; JEE Advanced papers have per-section marking schemes (partial marking, negative marking varying by section) which need a section-level scoring policy object anyway. Adopt shared stimulus as a real entity: JEE Advanced comprehension/paragraph questions and NEET assertion-reason sets share a stem across 2–3 items, and duplicating that stem is how banks drift out of sync. Do not attempt full QTI XML compliance — it is enormous — but do make the internal JSON schema mechanically convertible to QTI, because institutional buyers (schools, coaching chains) will eventually ask for import/export, and retrofitting is far more expensive than aligning names now.

recommendations: Make item immutability a database invariant, not a convention. Three tables: `questions` (stable identity, org-prefixed slug per QTI identifier guidance), `question_versions` (immutable content blob, version_no, status, created_by, approved_by with CHECK approved_by <> created_by, published_at), and `test_questions` / `attempt_responses` that both foreign-key to `question_version_id`. Rule to encode in the API layer: any change to stem, options, or key forks a new version and zeroes statistics; metadata-only changes (chapter re-tag, PYQ year, solution typo) may update in place. A RETIRED version is never deleted — past attempts depend on it. This single decision is what makes the platform defensible when a student disputes a rank.

Build ingestion as a two-stage hybrid with a mandatory human verification gate, and instrument the correction rate. Stage 1: Mathpix v3/pdf at $0.005/page (or a self-hosted Marker/Surya GPU worker on GCP at ~2.9–5.35 pages/s, subject to the Rail-M commercial licence above $5M revenue) to get LaTeX + layout. Stage 2: a vision LLM over the page image PLUS the stage-1 text, emitting {stem_latex, options[], correct_index, chapter_guess, difficulty_guess, has_diagram, diagram_bbox, pyq_year, source_provenance} — use the Batch API (50% cheaper) for archival back-catalogue and sync calls for the interactive admin flow. Every extracted item lands in status=DRAFT with a side-by-side original-crop vs rendered-LaTeX diff view. Track `edits_per_ingested_item` as the north-star metric for the whole content operation; it is the only honest measure of whether ingestion is actually saving money.

Adopt the QTI 3.0 Usage Data vocabulary verbatim for psychometrics, and scope every statistic to a context. Table: `item_statistics(question_version_id, context_id, statistic_name, value, case_count, std_error, std_deviation, computed_at)` with statistic_name drawn from {P-value, PTbis, AIS, A-Param, B-Param, C-Param} and a parallel `distractor_statistics` using {NumberChoosingResponse, PercentChoosingResponse, AISResponse, PTbis-Response}. context_id identifies the cohort/administration — the same item legitimately has different p-values for a JEE Main cohort and a NEET cohort. Recompute nightly via a scheduled job over Postgres (these are cheap aggregate queries), gated on case_count >= 100. Separately, keep `authored_difficulty` and `empirical_difficulty_p` as distinct columns, since QTI 3.0 deliberately excludes authored difficulty from its metadata profile — the delta between them is itself an author-calibration signal.

Ship the auto-flag rule engine on day one, wired to a human review queue. Default rules, all requiring case_count >= 100: p < 0.25 (too hard / possibly broken); p > 0.90 (giveaway, no discrimination); point-biserial < 0 (negative discrimination); any distractor with point-biserial exceeding the keyed option's (suspected MISKEY — highest severity, page the subject lead); any distractor selected by <5% (dead distractor); any non-key distractor selected by >30% (ambiguous item). Publish the honest expectation to stakeholders using the Siriraj 14,238-item evidence: these thresholds catch ~85.7% of genuinely flawed items and miss ~14.3%, so student 'report this question' flags are not a redundant channel — they are the recall layer that catches what statistics cannot see. Merge both signals into one triage inbox with severity ordering, and record disposition (RETAIN / REVISE / RETIRE / RESCORE) as an auditable event. RESCORE must be a real, implemented operation — dropping a bad item and recomputing every affected student's score and rank — because you will need it within the first three mocks.

Expand RBAC to capability-based authorisation with enforced separation of duties: AUTHOR, REVIEWER, SUBJECT_LEAD (sole publisher for a subject), OPS/SUPPORT (flag triage, no content mutation), ANALYST (read-only), SUPER_ADMIN. Store roles in Supabase raw_app_meta_data (admin-controlled), never raw_user_meta_data (user-modifiable). Because JWT claims are cached until token refresh, verify destructive capabilities (PUBLISH, RETIRE, RESCORE) inside a SECURITY DEFINER RPC against the live database rather than trusting the token claim. Item lifecycle: DRAFT → IN_REVIEW → CHANGES_REQUESTED → APPROVED → PUBLISHED → FLAGGED → RETIRED. Apply Supabase's documented RLS performance rules throughout — subselect-wrapped auth.uid() (94–99% faster), TO authenticated on every policy (99.78%), indexes on every policy-referenced column (99.94%), and a precomputed user_subject_access table to avoid joins inside policies (99.78%).

Separate order randomisation from content randomisation, and be explicit about which one the leaderboard can survive. For any ranked mock: identical item set for all students; shuffle item order within section and option order within item, seeded deterministically by hash(test_id, user_id) so any student's exact paper is reproducible months later for dispute resolution — store the seed, never the materialised permutation. Redis is the right place for the seed-to-permutation cache and the leaderboard, not for the source of truth. Only introduce genuinely different item sets (parallel forms) if you also implement score equating against a common anchor set; otherwise ranks are not comparable and you will be unable to defend them. For unranked practice, content randomisation is free and desirable.

Implement blueprint-driven auto-assembly as a real MILP, not SQL heuristics. Model it with OR-Tools CP-SAT or HiGHS in a Python worker on GCP (a few thousand binary variables solves in well under a second). Constraints: exact item count per chapter per the JEE/NEET blueprint, difficulty distribution over empirical p with fallback to authored_difficulty for uncalibrated items, exclusion of anything the student saw in their last 3 tests, PYQ-year spread, answer-key balance, and — using the question_relations table — no two members of the same variant family in one paper. Expose it in the admin UI as a blueprint the subject lead saves and reuses, with a 'why did it pick this item' explanation panel and manual override, because auto-assembly that cannot be overridden will simply not be trusted.

Model translations as versioned children of the English version, not as sibling questions. `question_version_translations(question_version_id, lang_code, stem, options[], solution, translated_by, reviewed_by, status)`. Answer key, marks and correct_index live ONLY on the English parent — this encodes NTA's own rule that the English version is final on translation ambiguity. Constraints: a translation cannot publish unless its parent is published, and editing the parent invalidates all translations rather than silently leaving them stale. Render bilingually stacked on one screen (English block above regional block) to mirror the real bilingual booklet rather than offering a language toggle. Scope Hindi + English for launch; treat the other 11 NEET languages as a per-state expansion decision driven by NTA's geographic centre restrictions, since each additional language is a full editorial and review cost multiplier.

Put provenance on every item as a mandatory, non-nullable field: ORIGINAL / PYQ_NTA / LICENSED / THIRD_PARTY_UNCLEARED, with source_ref (paper, year, shift, question number). Enforce that THIRD_PARTY_UNCLEARED cannot be published — it must be rewritten and re-approved first. Section 52(1)(i) exempts reproduction 'as part of the questions to be answered in an examination', which is the strongest available position for PYQs, but a commercial subscription app is neither a teacher nor an examination body, and India uses enumerated fair dealing rather than open-ended fair use — so treat PYQ reuse as a managed risk with a takedown process, not as settled. Get a written opinion from an Indian IP counsel before launch; this is a $2–3k spend that protects the entire catalogue.

Build the duplicate-detection triad at ingest and surface it as a warning, never a hard block: SHA-256 of the LaTeX-normalised stem for exact matches; MinHash-LSH over character 5-grams at Jaccard >= ~0.8 for transcription variants of the same PYQ; pgvector cosine >= ~0.92 for semantic clones with changed numbers. For image-based items use dHash or pHash at hashsize=16 with a Hamming threshold calibrated on ~500 hand-labelled pairs from your own corpus (imagehash publishes no accuracy figures, so vendor defaults are meaningless here). Persist results in `question_relations(a_id, b_id, kind, score)` with kind ∈ {EXACT_DUPLICATE, NEAR_DUPLICATE, VARIANT_OF, SUPERSEDES} — VARIANT_OF is an asset that feeds test assembly, not just a defect to purge.
pitfalls: Letting a delivered test reference a mutable question_id. The moment an admin fixes a typo in a live question, every historical attempt's rendered content silently changes, all accumulated statistics become meaningless, and you lose the ability to reconstruct what a student actually saw. This is unrecoverable retroactively — you cannot reconstruct pre-edit content from an audit log of diffs at scale. Decide it before the first mock test ships.

Computing a global p-value per question. Difficulty is population-dependent by definition (QTI's own spec calls P-value 'a group-dependent measure'), so a question that is p=0.70 for a NEET cohort may be p=0.30 for a JEE Advanced cohort, and a single blended number is worse than no number because admins will act on it. Every statistic needs a context/cohort scope from the first schema migration.

Displaying Cronbach's alpha without controlling for test length or cohort homogeneity. Alpha rises mechanically with item count, so a 25-question chapter drill will look 'unreliable' next to a 180-question mock even when its items are better, and a top-rankers-only batch will show depressed alpha purely through range restriction. Admins will draw exactly the wrong conclusion. Either suppress alpha below ~20 items, normalise via Spearman-Brown, or lead with SEM in raw-mark units instead.

Auto-retiring items on statistical flags. A 2025 study of 14,238 items found static thresholds miss 14.3% of genuinely flawed items while also flagging items that are legitimately hard — automatic retirement would both delete good hard questions and leave broken ones live. Flags must open a review task assigned to a subject lead, with a recorded disposition. Equally, having no RESCORE capability at all is its own failure: when you do drop a bad item mid-series, you must be able to recompute affected scores and ranks, and retrofitting that into a leaderboard built on denormalised Redis totals is very painful.

Adopting Surya/Marker weights without reading the licence. Code is Apache 2.0 but weights are a modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M free only for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue. An ed-tech company that raises a Series A silently becomes non-compliant across its entire ingestion pipeline. Decide early: pay Mathpix ($0.005/page — negligible at any realistic volume), buy the Datalab commercial licence, or restrict yourself to MIT-licensed pix2tex (which reports only 0.60 token accuracy and handles single formulas, not pages).

Randomising question CONTENT per student on a ranked mock. Different students receiving different items destroys rank comparability unless you implement parallel-form assembly with statistical matching and score equating — a substantial psychometric project. Randomising presentation order is safe; randomising content is not. Teams routinely conflate the two because both are called 'randomisation' in the requirements doc, and the damage only becomes visible when a parent disputes a rank.

Treating Hindi/regional questions as separate rows in the questions table. The moment the English version is corrected, translations silently diverge, and because the answer key exists in multiple places the translations can end up keyed differently from the parent — which is the single worst failure mode in a bilingual exam product. NTA's own rule (English is final on ambiguity) is the design instruction: keys and marks live only on the parent.

Shipping a two-role system and retrofitting workflow later. Once 20,000 items exist with created_by pointing at a single shared admin account, you cannot reconstruct who authored or approved anything, which destroys the audit trail exactly when you need it (a disputed key on a high-stakes mock). Separation of duties (approved_by <> created_by) is nearly free to add on day one and effectively impossible to backfill.

Using Google Document AI or Azure Document Intelligence for question ingestion because they are already in the cloud contract. Neither emits LaTeX; Custom Extraction at $30/1,000 pages is 15x Mathpix's PDF rate for a strictly worse result on mathematics. Reserve them for non-question document flows if at all.

Building admin analytics as ad-hoc queries against the live transactional tables. At 10k concurrent students the attempt_responses table grows by millions of rows per test, and a subject lead opening a chapter heatmap will lock up the same Postgres instance serving the exam. Precompute into summary tables on a schedule, or push analytics to a read replica / BigQuery on the GCP side.
openQuestions: Is NTA a 'Government' body for the purposes of Section 2(k) 'Government work' and Section 17(d) of the Copyright Act 1957? NTA is a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, which likely means its papers are NOT Government work and copyright vests in NTA itself. I could not verify this — the India Code PDF and copyright.gov.in returned 403/404. This materially changes the PYQ risk assessment and needs an Indian IP counsel opinion.

What did the Delhi High Court Division Bench actually hold in Chancellor Masters of Oxford v Rameshwari Photocopy Services (the DU photocopy case) about whether 'in the course of instruction' extends to a commercial third party acting for an educational institution? I could not retrieve the judgment (Indian Kanoon and SpicyIP fetches failed). This is the single most important precedent for whether a commercial app can lean on Section 52(1)(i) at all.

NCERT's exact copyright and reproduction policy — both ncert.nic.in/copyright.php and /copyright-policy.php returned 404. NCERT textbooks carry a standard 'no part of this publication may be reproduced' notice, and NCERT content underpins the entire NEET syllabus, so whether NCERT diagrams and passages can be reproduced in solutions is a live question. Unverified.

Canvas New Quizzes item-bank semantics: specifically whether editing a bank item propagates to already-delivered quizzes or whether the quiz holds a snapshot. My fetch of the Instructure community guide 404'd after redirect and the web-search budget was exhausted. This matters because Canvas is the most likely comparison point for an institutional buyer.

Mathpix's actual accuracy on Indian coaching-material scans specifically — low-quality photocopies, Devanagari mixed with LaTeX, hand-drawn physics free-body diagrams. Mathpix publishes no accuracy figure at all. This can only be answered by running a 200-page pilot against your own real source material and measuring edits-per-item.

Minimum sample size for IRT calibration (Rasch/1PL vs 2PL vs 3PL) — conventional guidance is roughly 100–200 for Rasch, 500+ for 2PL and 1000+ for 3PL, but I could not verify this against a citable source (assess.com and Taylor & Francis both returned 403). This determines whether IRT is viable at all at 10k students, or whether classical test theory is the only defensible option for the first year.

Whether JEE Main's regional-language offering matches NEET's 13. JEE Main has historically offered 13 languages including English, Hindi and regional options, but I verified only the NEET list. Confirm against the current JEE Main information bulletin before scoping translation work.

How Indian coaching institutes (Allen, Aakash, FIITJEE, PW) actually staff and run their internal item-authoring operations — team sizes, items authored per editor per day, review ratios. No public source found; this is competitive intelligence best obtained by hiring an ex-content-lead from one of them, and it directly determines the realistic throughput assumptions for the editorial workflow.

Whether QTI 3.0 import/export is a genuine purchase driver for Indian institutional buyers (coaching chains, schools) or a Western-market concern only. This determines whether to align the internal schema to QTI names now (cheap) or ignore the standard entirely.

Empirically calibrated thresholds for the duplicate-detection triad on Indian PYQ corpora specifically — the Jaccard 0.8 / cosine 0.92 / Hamming values I recommend are reasonable starting points from general literature, not tuned figures. They need calibration on ~500 hand-labelled pairs from the actual bank.
